title: IB Spanish B Exam Technique for November
summary: IB Spanish B exam technique for November: master writing, listening, reading and oral assessment with a focused three-week revision plan.
body_markdown:
Three weeks before the November session, Spanish can feel strangely unstable. One day, you understand a podcast almost effortlessly. The next, a reading passage seems to contain nothing but unfamiliar idioms.


That fluctuation is normal. At this stage, progress depends less on collecting more vocabulary and more on controlling what you already know under timed conditions. Effective **IB Spanish B exam technique** means reading the task precisely, recognising how marks are awarded and making deliberate decisions when comprehension is incomplete.


This guide follows a student through the final three weeks. It covers the current assessment components for both SL and HL, while recognising that schools may schedule the internally assessed individual oral before the written November examinations. Always confirm your exact timetable and administrative arrangements with your coordinator.


### The Spanish B assessment at a glance


Under the current Language B course, the final result is divided between productive, receptive and interactive language skills.


Component SL HL Weighting


Paper 1: writing 1 hour 15 minutes, one task, 250-400 words 1 hour 30 minutes, one task, 450-600 words 25%


Paper 2: listening 45 minutes 1 hour 25%


Paper 2: reading 1 hour 1 hour 25%


Individual oral 12-15 minutes, plus 15 minutes' preparation 12-15 minutes, plus 20 minutes' preparation 25%


Paper 1 presents three tasks drawn from the course themes. You choose one and select an appropriate text type from the options provided. Paper 2 assesses listening and reading through separate receptive-skills sections. At HL, the individual oral begins from an extract from one of the literary works studied; at SL, it begins from a visual stimulus connected to a course theme.


These details reflect the current Language B assessment model. Because the IB periodically revises subjects, use the guide and examination information supplied by your school as the final authority for your session.


### Your three-week checklist


- Diagnose weaknesses with one timed writing task and one listening-reading set.
- Build a small bank of flexible structures, not memorised essays.
- Practise identifying audience, purpose, context and text type.
- Review errors by cause rather than merely counting marks.
- Rehearse oral answers aloud every day.
- Complete full timed practice in Exam mode during the final week.


### Three weeks out: learn where marks are really lost


Imagine a student opening their first timed task on a Monday afternoon. The temptation is to begin writing immediately. That feels productive, but it conceals the most common strategic error: answering the general topic rather than the exact prompt.


Paper 1 is assessed through language, message and conceptual understanding. In practical terms, examiners want accurate and varied Spanish, relevant development of every required element, and a response suited to its audience, purpose and context. An elegant article that ignores one bullet point is still incomplete.


Before writing, underline four things:


- **Audience:** Who will read this?
- **Purpose:** Are you informing, persuading, reflecting or proposing?
- **Context:** What situation created the text?
- **Required content:** Which explicit points must appear?


Then choose the text type that performs those jobs naturally. A formal proposal needs recommendations, logical organisation and an appropriately professional register. A blog entry usually invites a more personal voice and direct engagement with readers. A speech should sound speakable, with an opening address and rhetorical movement.


Use the first 5-8 minutes to plan. Assign each required point to a paragraph and note two useful structures beside it. During the final 8-10 minutes, check verb endings, gender agreement, accents, register and whether every instruction has been answered.


The[RevisionDojo guide to the new IB Language B assessment structure](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/new-ib-language-b-assessment-structure) offers a useful assessment overview. For day-to-day work, use the RevisionDojo Questionbank to practise one task type at a time, then compare your response with the criteria using the Grading tools.


### Two weeks out: turn Paper 2 into a process


Receptive skills reward evidence, not vague understanding. You may grasp the overall meaning of a recording or article yet lose marks because an answer lacks the precise detail requested.


### Listening technique


Before the audio begins, read ahead. Circle interrogatives such as *por qué* , *cómo* , *cuándo* and *qué ventaja* . They predict the information you need. Mark whether an answer appears to require a person, reason, place, number or attitude.


On the first hearing, establish the situation and track likely answer locations. On the second, confirm details and resolve uncertainty. Do not spend so much attention translating one unknown word that the recording moves beyond you. Meaning often sits in contrast markers such as *sin embargo* , *aunque* , *en cambio* and *por lo tanto* .


For multiple-choice questions, eliminate options contradicted by the audio. For short responses, answer only what is asked and preserve the meaning accurately. If instructions permit answers in the target language, keep your Spanish concise rather than creating avoidable grammar problems.


Two students discover that hearing every word is less useful than answering the question


### Reading technique


Start with the questions, then scan the text for names, dates, repeated nouns and synonyms. The wording in a question may paraphrase the passage, so searching for an identical phrase is unreliable.


For reference questions, check the noun or idea immediately before the pronoun and test whether the meaning remains logical. For true-or-false style items that request justification, the justification is essential. Copy only the words that prove the decision rather than an entire paragraph.


Vocabulary-in-context questions are not dictionary tests. Substitute each possible meaning into the sentence, then check tone and surrounding ideas. When matching headings, identify the paragraph's central function, not its most memorable detail.


After each practice set, label mistakes as vocabulary, attention, inference, time management or misunderstood instructions. RevisionDojo Study Notes and Flashcards can repair a vocabulary gap. AI Chat can explain why a particular answer follows from the text. The distinction matters because rereading vocabulary will not fix careless evidence selection.


### Ten days out: make the oral structured, not scripted


The strongest oral preparation creates dependable movement without producing a memorised monologue.


For SL, organise your visual response around description, interpretation and thematic connection. Describe only details you can see, infer what they may suggest and connect them to Spanish-speaking cultures or communities where relevant. Avoid treating cultural knowledge as decoration. It should deepen your interpretation.


For HL, locate the literary extract within the work, analyse significant choices and connect the passage to a course theme. Brief quotation or precise reference is more persuasive than retelling the plot.


In the discussion, extend answers through a simple pattern:


1. State your view clearly.
2. Give a reason or example.
3. Add a qualification, consequence or contrasting perspective.


If you do not understand a question, ask for clarification in Spanish. That is usually more effective than guessing the topic. Useful phrases include *¿Podría repetir la pregunta?* and *¿Se refiere a...?*


Record two-minute responses on the five prescribed themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. Listen for repeated words, unfinished sentences and tense control. RevisionDojo Tutors can provide live conversational feedback, while AI Chat can generate follow-up questions for independent rehearsal.


### The final week: practise decisions under pressure


The final week is not the moment to rebuild your entire Spanish vocabulary. It is the moment to make exam behaviour familiar.


Sit one complete writing task and full receptive-skills practice under accurate timing. Use Questionbank material and complete timed papers in RevisionDojo's Exam mode, without pausing to search for vocabulary. Mock Exams and Predicted Papers can add realistic pressure, but their greatest value comes from the review afterwards.


For every lost mark, write one corrective rule. For example:


- I answered *what happened* but the question asked *why* .
- I selected an unsuitable register for the audience.
- I copied too much text and obscured the required evidence.
- I used complex grammar without controlling the verb.


Two days before the examination, reduce the volume. Review your text-type conventions, flexible connectors and personal error list. Speak Spanish briefly, but do not exhaust yourself with a full mock late at night.


### On the day of the November exam


Read every instruction before committing to a response. In Paper 1, choose the task that gives you the clearest content and text-type fit, not simply the most familiar topic. In Paper 2, keep moving and return to uncertain items when the format allows.


Most importantly, do not interpret one difficult passage as evidence that the whole examination is going badly. Difficulty is shared. Marks are earned one decision at a time.


That is the quiet advantage of good preparation. Three weeks earlier, the student was trying to know everything. By November, they have learned something more useful: how to show what they know.
